section.title: Elisha's Miracles
section.sectionRationale: A cluster of five episodes shows Elisha's ministry moving among ordinary, needy people: a widow drowning in debt, a childless woman of Shunem who receives and then loses and regains a son, a poisoned pot of stew, and a small provision of bread that feeds a hundred men with some left over. Each miracle answers real, desperate lack with the LORD's abundant provision through His prophet.
section.thesis: Through Elisha the LORD meets debt, barrenness, death, poison, and famine alike with overflowing provision, proving that no need is too small or too great for the God who sent him.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the widow's multiplied oil, verses 1 to 7; the Shunammite's promised and then restored son, verses 8 to 37; the purified stew, verses 38 to 41; and the multiplied bread, verses 42 to 44.

units.label: The widow's oil
units.note: sell the oil and pay your debt

verses.text: Now the wife of one of the sons of the prophets cried out to Elisha, "Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that your servant feared the LORD. And now his creditor is coming to take my two children as his slaves!"
"How can I help you?" asked Elisha. "Tell me, what do you have in the house?" She answered, "Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of {{shemen|oil}}."
"Go," said Elisha, "borrow empty jars from all your neighbors. Do not gather just a few.
Then go inside, shut the door behind you and your sons, and pour oil into all these jars, setting the full ones aside."
So she left him, and after she had shut the door behind her and her sons, they kept bringing jars to her, and she kept pouring.
When all the jars were full, she said to her son, "Bring me another." But he replied, "There are no more jars." Then the oil stopped flowing.
She went and told the man of God, and he said, "Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt. Then you and your sons can live on the remainder."
One day Elisha went to Shunem, and a prominent woman who lived there persuaded him to have a meal. So whenever he would pass by, he would stop there to eat.
Then the woman said to her husband, "Behold, now I know that the one who often comes our way is a holy man of God.
Please let us make a small room upstairs and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for him. Then when he comes to us, he can stay there."
One day Elisha came to visit and went to his upper room to lie down.
And he said to Gehazi his servant, "Call the Shunammite woman." And when he had called her, she stood before him,

and Elisha said to Gehazi, "Now tell her, 'Look, you have gone to all this trouble for us. What can we do for you? Can we speak on your behalf to the king or the commander of the army?'" "I have a home among my own people," she replied.
So he asked, "Then what should be done for her?" "Well, she has no son," Gehazi replied, "and her husband is old."
"Call her," said Elisha. So Gehazi called her, and she stood in the doorway.
And Elisha declared, "At this time next year, you will hold a {{ben|son}} in your arms." "No, my lord," she said. "Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God."
But the woman did conceive, and at that time the next year she gave birth to a son, just as Elisha had told her.

units.label: The Shunammite's son dies and is raised

verses.text: And the child grew, and one day he went out to his father, who was with the harvesters.
"My head! My head!" he complained to his father. So his father told a servant, "Carry him to his mother."
After the servant had picked him up and carried him to his mother, the boy sat on her lap until noon, and then he died.
And she went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God. Then she shut the door and went out.
And the woman called her husband and said, "Please send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, that I may go quickly to the man of God and return."
"Why would you go to him today?" he replied. "It is not a New Moon or a Sabbath." "Everything is all right," she said.
Then she saddled the donkey and told her servant, "Drive onward; do not slow the pace for me unless I tell you."
So she set out and went to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her at a distance, he said to his servant Gehazi, "Look, there is the Shunammite woman.
Please run out now to meet her and ask, 'Are you all right? Is your husband all right? Is your child all right?'" And she answered, "Everything is all right."

When she reached the man of God at the mountain, she clung to his feet. Gehazi came over to push her away, but the man of God said, "Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me."
Then she said, "Did I ask you for a son, my lord? Didn't I say, 'Do not deceive me?'"

So Elisha said to Gehazi, "Tie up your garment, take my staff in your hand, and go! If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not answer him. Then lay my staff on the boy's face."
And the mother of the boy said, "As surely as the LORD {{chai|lives}} and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So he got up and followed her.
Gehazi went on ahead of them and laid the staff on the boy's face, but there was no sound or response. So he went back to meet Elisha and told him, "The boy has not awakened."
When Elisha reached the house, there was the boy lying dead on his bed.
So he went in, closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD.
Then Elisha got on the bed and lay on the boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, and hand to hand. As he stretched himself out over him, the boy's body became warm.
Elisha turned away and paced back and forth across the room. Then he got on the bed and stretched himself out over the boy again, and the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
Elisha summoned Gehazi and said, "Call the Shunammite woman." So he called her and she came. Then Elisha said, "Pick up your son."
She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.

units.label: The purified stew and the multiplied bread
units.note: there is nothing harmful in the pot

verses.text: When Elisha returned to Gilgal, there was a famine in the land. As the sons of the prophets were sitting at his feet, he said to his attendant, "Put on the large pot and boil some stew for the sons of the prophets."

One of them went out to the field to gather herbs, and he found a wild vine from which he gathered as many wild gourds as his garment could hold. Then he came back and cut them up into the pot of stew, though no one knew what they were.
And they poured it out for the men to eat, but when they tasted the stew they cried out, "There is {{maveth|death}} in the pot, O man of God!" And they could not eat it.
Then Elisha said, "Get some flour." He threw it into the pot and said, "Pour it out for the people to eat." And there was nothing harmful in the pot.
Now a man from Baal-shalishah came to the man of God with a sack of twenty loaves of barley bread from the first ripe grain. "Give it to the people to eat," said Elisha.
But his servant asked, "How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?" "Give it to the people to eat," said Elisha, "for this is what the LORD says: 'They will eat and have some left over.'"
So he set it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of the LORD.

shemen.gloss: Oil, a staple good used for cooking, light, and anointing, and here the widow's only remaining asset. The LORD multiplies this small, ordinary resource until it exceeds every container she can find, stopping only when the vessels run out, not the oil itself.

ben.gloss: Son. A ben was central to a family's future, inheritance, and security in ancient Israel; the childless Shunammite's disbelief, do not lie to your maidservant, shows how far beyond hope Elisha's promise of a ben seemed to her.

maveth.gloss: Death. The prophets' cry, there is death in the pot, uses the same word Scripture uses for mortal danger generally; Elisha's simple act of adding flour turns maveth into safe food, a small but vivid picture of the LORD overturning death itself.

chai.gloss: Living or alive, the root behind the Shunammite's oath, as surely as the LORD lives. Her insistence not to leave Elisha until he came to her dying son echoes Elisha's own earlier vow never to leave Elijah, 2:2, 4, 6, binding master and disciple in the same persistent faith.

basic.context: This chapter gathers four scenes from Elisha's daily ministry among ordinary people. A prophet's widow, facing the loss of her sons into slavery for debt, receives multiplied oil from Elisha's word. A wealthy but childless woman of Shunem who has shown Elisha hospitality is promised, and then given, a son, who later dies of what sounds like heatstroke, and whom Elisha raises back to life after her urgent, faith-filled pursuit of him. A poisoned stew is purified with a handful of flour, and twenty loaves unexpectedly feed a hundred men with food left over.
basic.hermeneutics: These are historical accounts of specific miraculous acts through God's prophet; they are not formulas guaranteeing that every debt, illness, or hunger will be solved by ritual actions like pouring oil or adding flour. What endures is the character of the God who acts through Elisha: attentive to the desperate, generous beyond human resources, and able to reverse even death.
basic.originalLanguages: The widow's only asset is shemen, oil, which the LORD multiplies until every borrowed vessel is full. The childless Shunammite is promised a ben, son, a gift so far beyond her expectation that she initially disbelieves it. When death, maveth, appears to fill the prophets' pot, Elisha's simple act makes it safe again. And the Shunammite's urgent oath, as surely as the LORD, chai, lives, echoes the same persistent faith Elisha himself once showed toward Elijah.
basic.typology: The oil that overflows every vessel brought to it, the son given against all natural hope and then raised from death, and the food that multiplies beyond its natural supply all anticipate the greater abundance and resurrection life that Christ alone fully provides.
basic.christ: Elisha stretching himself over the dead child until warmth and life return anticipates Christ, who took on our death fully so that resurrection life might flow from Him into those who are spiritually dead, Ephesians 2:1-5. The multiplied loaves that fed a hundred with some left over directly foreshadow Jesus feeding thousands from a few loaves, John 6:1-13, revealing the same LORD of abundant provision at work in a greater Prophet.
basic.god: God is attentive to every scale of human need, from a widow's household debt to a family's grief over a dead child to hungry prophets facing a poisoned meal and a famine. He is not a distant deity but One who multiplies the little that is offered to Him and who has power even over death, displayed here through His servant Elisha before it is displayed fully in Christ.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 17:8-24 gives Elijah's earlier, similar provision of flour and oil for a widow and his raising of her son, the pattern Elisha now continues and extends. 2 Kings 8:1-6 later resumes the Shunammite woman's story, showing the LORD's continued care for her family. John 6:1-13 explicitly parallels the multiplication of loaves, and Mark 5:35-43 parallels Elisha's raising of the dead child.
basic.oneStory: These small, intimate miracles rehearse on a household scale the whole story the Bible tells: the LORD meets impossible debt, hopeless barrenness, sudden death, hidden poison, and real hunger with abundant, gracious provision, all anticipating the greater and final provision and resurrection secured for God's people in Jesus Christ.

context.literary:
Chapter 4 is an anthology rather than a single continuous scene, four self contained vignettes stitched together only by the recurring title the man of God and by Elisha's habit of turning to ordinary households right after the failed, morally compromised campaign against Moab that fills chapter 3. Each vignette opens with a bare narrative marker, now, one day, when Elisha returned, signalling a fresh episode rather than a continuous timeline, a technique used throughout the surrounding material to gather the Elisha traditions into a loosely bound cycle of independent reports.

Within that anthology, the second and longest unit, the Shunammite's son, verses 8 to 37, is shaped with real symmetry. A woman who asks for nothing, verse 13, is given far more than she imagined, verse 17, then loses what she was given, verse 20, and must travel with mounting urgency, saddle the donkey, do not slow the pace, to recover it, verses 22 to 25, before the gift is restored through repeated, physical effort, verses 32 to 35. The refrain everything is all right, spoken twice by the woman while concealing a catastrophe, verses 23 and 26, is a deliberate irony that only resolves when Elisha finally learns the truth in verse 27.

The final two miracles, the stew and the loaves, are compressed almost to formula, he said, they poured it out, nothing harmful, give it to the people, they ate and had some left over, a terseness that suits the ordinary, almost domestic setting of a communal kitchen rather than a royal court. Read together, the four scenes widen in scope, from one widow's household, to one family's grief, to a whole company of prophets, tracing an arc of expanding provision that prepares the reader for the still larger national deliverances of chapters 5 to 7.
context.historical:
The widow's crisis reflects a real and harsh legal exposure. A creditor could seize a debtor's children as bonded labour until the debt was worked off, a practice Israel's own law limited but did not abolish, requiring release at the Jubilee, Leviticus 25:39-41, and echoed later in Nehemiah 5:2-5 when families under Persian rule faced the identical threat from their own countrymen. That her husband had belonged to the sons of the prophets matters too, these were organised communities of prophetic disciples, evidently supported partly by their own labour, poor enough that a single jar of oil was the household's whole remaining estate.

Shunem sat in the fertile Jezreel Valley on a natural route between the coast and the Jordan, which is likely why Elisha, itinerant by habit, passed by often enough for a resident family to notice the pattern and build him a dedicated roof chamber, furnished simply with a bed, table, chair and lamp, the standard fittings of a modest guest room in this period. The boy's collapse with the harvesters in the heat of the grain harvest points to sunstroke, a documented hazard of fieldwork under the Israelite sun, and his death by noon fits the rapid course such a collapse can take without shade or water close at hand.

The famine at Gilgal and the description of the sons of the prophets sitting at his feet describe a settled teaching community large enough to need a communal pot, while the wild gourds gathered in ignorance reflect a genuine local danger, certain wild vines in the region bear a bitter, purgative fruit that an inexperienced forager could easily mistake for something edible. The gift of twenty loaves of barley bread from the first ripe grain in the final scene evokes the custom of bringing firstfruits to a man of God, barley being the earliest and humblest grain harvested, the ordinary bread of the poor rather than a delicacy.
context.canonical:
This chapter's closest relative is 1 Kings 17:8-24, where Elijah supplies a widow's food from a jar that never runs dry and later revives her dead son by stretching himself over the boy three times. Elisha's ministry deliberately repeats both signs almost move for move, oil that outlasts every vessel, a body warmed by repeated physical contact, confirming the double portion of Elijah's spirit he asked for at the Jordan, 2 Kings 2:9-14. The pattern does not stop with Elisha's own lifetime. 2 Kings 13:20-21 records a dead man restored to life merely by touching Elisha's bones years after his burial, so the Shunammite's son turns out to be the first of three resurrections that bracket Elisha's whole career.

The Shunammite herself is not left behind at the end of the chapter. 2 Kings 8:1-6 resumes her story during a seven year famine, and it is Gehazi, the very servant whose staff failed to revive her son here, verse 31, who happens to be recounting Elisha's great deeds to the king at the exact moment she arrives to beg for her land back, so that her case is settled on the spot by what looks like coincidence but reads as providence. The narrative binds chapter 4 and chapter 8 together across an intervening span of years.

Later Scripture treats this whole complex of provision and resurrection miracles as a rehearsal for something greater. Jesus multiplies loaves for crowds in all four Gospels, and Mark 5:35-43 and Luke 7:11-17 both record him raising a dead child and a widow's only son, deliberately recalling the Elijah and Elisha pattern for readers who already knew these chapters well.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The compiler of Kings places this cluster of intimate miracles directly after the failed campaign against Moab in chapter 3, a deliberate contrast. National politics under Jehoram accomplishes little and ends in Israel's own retreat, 3:27, while Elisha's quiet ministry among nameless households accomplishes everything it sets out to do. Original hearers, living under kings whose military and religious leadership repeatedly disappointed, were meant to see where real, reliable power actually rested, not in royal armies but in the word of the LORD spoken through his prophet.

Each miracle also authenticates Elisha specifically as Elijah's covenant heir. The double portion he requested in 2:9 is not an abstract spiritual gift, it is demonstrated here through the exact categories Elijah exercised in 1 Kings 17, provision from a nearly empty vessel and the raising of a dead child, proving to a watching, sceptical audience, note the Shunammite's blunt do not deceive me and do not lie to your maidservant, that Elisha's authority is genuine continuation and not self appointed imitation. The narrator wants readers to trust this prophet's later, larger pronouncements, chapters 5 to 8, precisely because his character has already been proven in these small, verifiable, domestic scale wonders.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These four accounts describe specific historical interventions, not a manual for household economics or medicine. The widow's instruction to gather not just a few jars describes what faith looked like in her particular circumstance, it is not a formula implying that anyone facing debt should borrow containers and expect oil to multiply. Likewise Elisha's physical posture over the dead boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand, describes an act particular to this prophet and this moment, it is neither a resuscitation technique nor a guarantee that grief will always end in restoration in this life.

What the narrative does carry forward is a pattern of response rather than a method, desperate need brought honestly to God's appointed means, and obedience carried out fully rather than partially, she did not gather just a few jars, precisely because the limit of the miracle in each case was set by the recipient's own action, not by any shortage in God's supply. Readers today rightly ask what God can do with the little they bring him, without expecting oil or bread to multiply on command.

debates.question: Why did Elisha initially not know the cause of the Shunammite's distress, verse 27?

views.label: God selectively withholds knowledge from his prophets
views.case: The text states plainly that the LORD had hidden it from Elisha, showing that even a genuine prophet does not possess automatic, unlimited knowledge but only what God chooses to reveal at a given moment, a check against over exalting the prophetic office itself.

views.label: A narrative device that foregrounds the woman's own initiative
views.case: By leaving Elisha unaware, the story highlights the Shunammite's urgent, persistent pursuit of help, riding without slowing the pace and clinging to his feet, and shows that even in a crisis unknown to the prophet, faith presses forward toward God's appointed means.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm that Elisha's power was never automatic or self generated but entirely dependent on what the LORD chose to reveal and to do through him, which keeps the glory with God rather than with the prophet.

debates.question: Why did Gehazi's staff fail to revive the boy, verse 31, when Elisha himself succeeded?

views.label: The staff carried no power of its own
views.case: The narrative specifies there was no sound or response until Elisha himself arrived, prayed, and stretched out over the child, showing that resurrection life flowed from the LORD's presence and prayer, not from an object or a delegate, however loyal.

views.label: The Shunammite's own refusal to accept a substitute was part of the appointed means
views.case: Her vow, as surely as the LORD lives, I will not leave you, insisted on Elisha in person, and her insistence was itself the faith God had chosen to honour, so Gehazi's errand was never going to be the channel of the miracle.

debates.bearing: Either way the episode safeguards the same truth, that life returns only through the LORD's own word and presence, never through a technique, a staff, or a stand in, however faithful the messenger.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's most frequent title for Elisha is not his name but ish ha elohim, man of God, used well over a dozen times across these forty four verses, more often than his personal name. The same title describes Elijah throughout 1 Kings 17, so its repetition here is not incidental, it stakes Elisha's claim to Elijah's exact office before a single miracle is even performed.

The Shunammite is introduced in verse 8 as ishah gedolah, a great or prominent woman, the adjective gadol describing her standing and evidently her wealth. The same root resurfaces in 2 Kings 8:4, where Gehazi is asked to relate all the great things, haggedolot, Elisha has done, so the woman first called great becomes, four chapters later, part of the evidence for Elisha's own greatness, a quiet bracket around her whole story.

When the woman finally reaches Elisha at Carmel, verse 27 says her nephesh, her soul or her very self, is marah, bitter or in deep distress. The same pairing describes Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:10, bitter in soul, weeping before the LORD over her own childlessness, so Scripture uses one shared idiom for two women whose deepest grief concerns a son, one unable to conceive, the other unable to keep the son she was given.

That son was promised in language that pointedly echoes an earlier promise. Elisha's words in verse 16, at this time next year, translate the same Hebrew phrase, ka'et chayyah, that the LORD speaks to Abraham in Genesis 18:10 and 14 concerning Sarah, a phrase so close that both English translations land on nearly identical wording. The Shunammite's own disbelief, do not lie to your maidservant, mirrors Sarah's laughter in that same scene, Genesis 18:12, two women told of a son beyond their own power to produce him.

Finally, when the prophets cry maveth, death, in the pot, verse 40, the word is the blunt, ordinary term for mortal danger used across the Old Testament, not a technical term for poison, which sharpens the point that Elisha's handful of flour answers death itself, however small the scale, with the same authority that will later answer a boy's actual death in the very same chapter.

One small word ties several of these scenes together at the level of grammar rather than vocabulary. Elisha's characteristic instruction is the bare imperative lekh, go, go, borrow empty jars, verse 3, go, sell the oil, verse 7, and again, tie up your garment and go, when he sends Gehazi ahead with the staff, verse 29. The command is never accompanied by an explanation of how the miracle will work, only a concrete action to be carried out in faith, so that the shape of obedience across the chapter is consistently simple, immediate, and unaccompanied by proof in advance.

typology.type: Oil multiplied without limit from a small, ordinary supply, verses 1 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The widow's one remaining jar becomes enough to cancel her debt and support her household only because she keeps bringing empty vessels for it to fill. This anticipates the Spirit given without measure through Christ and the grace that keeps supplying grace upon grace to those who keep coming empty handed, John 1:16, John 3:34. The type is limited, though, since the oil still runs out once the jars run out; the supply Christ gives to those who trust him is never exhausted by any vessel brought to it.

typology.type: A dead child restored through the prophet's own bodily identification with him, verses 32 to 35
typology.fulfillment: Elisha does not merely speak from a distance, he lies on the boy twice, mouth to mouth, until warmth and then life return. This anticipates Christ's own death and resurrection, in which he fully entered human death so that resurrection life might flow from him into those united to him, Romans 6:5, 1 Corinthians 15:20-22. The type falls short in that Elisha needed to labour and pray for life to return, while Christ, once raised, needs no repetition and gives life by his own inherent authority.

typology.type: A small quantity of bread multiplied to feed many with abundance left over, verses 42 to 44
typology.fulfillment: Twenty loaves feed a hundred men because Elisha commands the bread be given out despite the servant's doubt that it could possibly be enough. This directly anticipates Jesus feeding five thousand and four thousand from a handful of loaves, John 6:1-13, Mark 8:1-9, revealing him as the true bread of life rather than merely a multiplier of bread, John 6:35. Where Elisha's multiplication met one crowd's hunger once, Christ offers himself as food that satisfies forever.

typology.type: Sons rescued from slavery for an unpayable debt, verses 1 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The widow's sons face bondage for a debt she cannot pay until the prophet's provision cancels it outright. This pictures the far greater rescue of those enslaved to a debt of sin they could never repay, whose record of debt Christ cancelled, nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:13-14, and whose redemption from bondage cost not a jar of oil but his own blood, Galatians 3:13. The type is partial, since the widow's debt was owed in silver, while the debt Christ cancels is owed in righteousness itself.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first by pattern. Elisha, called man of God like Elijah before him, repeats his master's exact miracles, oil that does not run out, a dead child restored, and the Gospels deliberately place Jesus in that same prophetic lineage while showing him surpass it at every point. Where Elisha needed to stretch himself over the boy twice and pace the room between attempts, verses 34 to 35, Jesus raises Jairus's daughter with a single sentence and a touch of the hand, Mark 5:41, and calls Lazarus, already four days dead, out of the tomb with a shout from outside it, John 11:43. The prophet must labour for life to return, the Son simply speaks and it is so.

It leads to Christ by provision. Elisha commands, give it to the people to eat, over his own servant's doubt that twenty loaves could feed a hundred men, and there is food left over, verses 43 to 44. Centuries later Jesus tells his own doubting disciples, you give them something to eat, Mark 6:37, over five loaves and two fish for five thousand, and twelve baskets are gathered up afterward, John 6:12-13. The doubt is the same, the abundance is greater, and this time the one commanding the bread is himself its ultimate source, I am the bread of life, John 6:35.

It leads to Christ by rescue. A widow's sons face slavery for a debt she cannot pay, and the prophet's word cancels it before it is executed. Paul later describes believers as those who once stood condemned by a certificate of debt that stood against them, until God cancelled it, nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14, and redeemed those under the law's debt at the price of his own Son, Galatians 4:4-5. What Elisha did for one household with a jar of oil, Christ does for every believer at infinite cost.

A word of caution keeps the reading honest. Not every detail, the borrowed jars, the seven sneezes, the wild gourds, is a coded picture of Jesus. What the chapter supplies is the shape of the problem, debt, barrenness, death, poison, hunger, and the first outline of the greater Prophet who would meet every one of them not by miracle alone but by becoming, in himself, the answer to each.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who is free in what he reveals and when. Elisha genuinely does not know the Shunammite's grief until she stands before him, verse 27, because the LORD has hidden it from him, a detail the narrator does not explain away. God's secrets belong to him, Deuteronomy 29:29, and even his own prophet learns only what God chooses to disclose, at the moment God chooses to disclose it, a safeguard against ever treating Elisha, or any prophetic office, as possessing automatic access to the divine mind.

He is also a God whose provision answers the precise shape of each need rather than a generic supply. The widow needed money, and received oil convertible to money. The Shunammite needed a son and, later, that son's life restored, and received exactly that, nothing more general. The prophets needed safe food, and received flour thrown into a poisoned pot, not a replacement meal. Hungry men needed bread, and received bread with some left over, not abstract sustenance. God's care in this chapter is not vague benevolence, it is attentive to detail.

He is a God who does not need visible resources to act. A single jar becomes enough for many vessels, twenty loaves become enough for a hundred men, because the limit on his provision was never the size of what he was given but the size of what people were willing to bring and to keep bringing. And he is a God who reverses death itself on a household scale here, prefiguring what he will do for the whole world, showing that no grief, however total it feels to the person carrying it, my head, my head, and then he died, verse 20, lies outside his power to answer.

Finally, this is a God who works through ordinary means, borrowed jars, a stick thrown into water, a handful of flour, without ever letting the means become the object of trust. The chapter keeps its eyes on the LORD who acts, not on Elisha's methods, and so it teaches worshippers to ask boldly and to watch for how, not whether, God will answer.

crossReferences.note: Elijah's earlier ministry to a widow, including flour and oil that do not run dry and the raising of her son by stretching over him three times, is the direct pattern Elisha now repeats almost move for move as Elijah's prophetic heir.

The Shunammite's story resumes years later during a seven year famine, and Gehazi happens to be recounting Elisha's great deeds to the king at the very moment she arrives to reclaim her land, so her case is settled by what reads as quiet providence.

A dead man is restored to life merely by touching Elisha's bones years after his burial, making the Shunammite's son the first of three resurrection accounts that bracket Elisha's entire prophetic career.

The law limited debt bondage among Israelites, requiring release at the Jubilee, showing that the widow's fear of losing her sons to a creditor was a real exposure under a system the LORD had already moved to restrain.

The LORD's promise to Abraham that Sarah would bear a son at this time next year is echoed almost word for word in Elisha's promise to the Shunammite, and both women answer with disbelief at a gift beyond their own power to produce.

Hannah's bitter soul before the LORD over her childlessness uses the same idiom later applied to the Shunammite's grief, linking two women whose deepest distress concerns a son, one unable to conceive and one unable to keep the son she received.

Jesus raises a widow's only son at Nain with a word and a touch of the coffin, deliberately recalling the Elijah and Elisha pattern of a prophet restoring a bereaved mother's son, while surpassing it by requiring no prayer or repeated effort.

Jesus tells his doubting disciples, you give them something to eat, over five loaves for five thousand, echoing the servant's doubt here that twenty loaves could feed a hundred, and again ending with abundance left over rather than a shortfall.
Paul describes believers as once condemned by a record of debt that God cancelled and nailed to the cross, the pattern the widow's rescued sons foreshadow on a much smaller, household scale.

study.oneStory:
Since Genesis 3 the world has lived under scarcity and death, thorns instead of easy fruit, toil instead of rest, and finally dust returning to dust. This chapter shows the LORD reversing that curse in miniature, in exactly the categories it created, debt, barrenness, death, danger in food, and hunger, refusing to leave any one of them untouched.

Nothing here happens through royal power. The kings of Israel and Aram are fighting wars in the surrounding chapters that accomplish little, while the LORD's real work unfolds in a widow's house, a guest room in Shunem, and a common pot at Gilgal, confirming a pattern that runs through the whole of Scripture, God's greatest acts rarely happen at the centre of worldly power. The same LORD who fed Israel with manna in the wilderness and multiplied a widow's flour for Elijah now multiplies oil and bread for Elisha, and will one day feed thousands through his own Son.

The chapter also anticipates what still lies ahead. Death is undone here for one family, briefly, and at a cost of great labour and prayer, a signpost rather than the final answer. The gospel will show death undone permanently, at the cost of the Saviour's own life rather than a prophet's effort, and the new creation will complete what these miracles only sketch, no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and a tree whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2, a permanent answer to every hunger, every debt, and every grief this chapter meets only for a season.

Read this way, four small household miracles are not a detour from the Bible's main story but a rehearsal of it in a single family's crises, preparing readers to recognise the same character, the same patience with doubt, the same abundance out of almost nothing, when it appears fully in Jesus Christ.

quiz.q: How did Elisha help the prophet's widow facing the loss of her sons to a creditor?

options.text: He had her borrow many empty jars and pour her one remaining jar of oil into them until it miraculously filled every vessel, providing money to pay her debt.
options.note: Verses 2 to 7 record this exact miracle and its purpose.

options.text: He personally paid off her debt from his own resources.
options.note: The text describes a miracle of multiplied oil, not a direct cash payment from Elisha.

options.text: He told her to sell her sons into service temporarily.
options.note: The whole point of the miracle was to prevent her sons from being taken as slaves, not to arrange it.

options.text: He told her the debt would simply be forgiven with no action required.
options.note: Elisha instructed specific action, gathering jars and pouring oil, which she had to obey in faith.

quiz.q: What did Elisha promise the childless Shunammite woman, and how did she initially respond?

options.text: He promised she would hold a son in her arms within a year, and she disbelieved him, saying, do not lie to your maidservant.
options.note: Verse 16 records both the promise and her skeptical response.

options.text: She immediately believed and thanked him joyfully.
options.note: The text records her initial disbelief, not immediate joyful acceptance.

options.text: He promised her wealth rather than a child.
options.note: The specific promise concerned a son, not material wealth.

options.text: She had already asked Elisha for this exact promise.
options.note: The promise came unprompted; she had not requested a son from Elisha.

quiz.q: How did Elisha respond when the Shunammite's son died, and what did he do to restore him?

options.text: He went to the boy, prayed, and stretched himself over the body repeatedly until the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
options.note: Verses 33 to 35 describe this specific process leading to the boy's revival.

options.text: He simply spoke a word from a distance and the boy revived instantly.
options.note: The text describes physical, repeated, intimate action, prayer and stretching over the boy, not a distant spoken word alone.

options.text: He refused to help until the woman paid him.
options.note: No payment is mentioned; Elisha responded to her urgent plea and went with her immediately.

options.text: The boy could not be revived and remained dead.
options.note: The text explicitly records the boy's revival, sneezing seven times and opening his eyes.

quiz.q: How did Elisha resolve the danger of the poisoned stew at Gilgal?

options.text: He had flour thrown into the pot, after which there was nothing harmful in it and the people could eat safely.
options.note: Verses 40 to 41 record this exact resolution.

options.text: He commanded the men to simply throw the whole pot away.
options.note: Elisha's actual solution restored the food rather than discarding it entirely.

options.text: He identified the wild gourds and removed them one by one.
options.note: The text does not describe manual removal of the gourds; flour was added to the whole pot instead.

options.text: The stew remained dangerous and no one could eat it.
options.note: The text explicitly states there was nothing harmful in the pot afterward.

quiz.q: What happened when twenty loaves of barley bread were set before a hundred men?

options.text: According to the LORD's word through Elisha, the men ate and had food left over, despite the servant's doubt that so little bread could feed so many.
options.note: Verses 42 to 44 record the servant's doubt and the miraculous outcome exactly as Elisha declared.

options.text: The bread ran out before all the men could eat.
options.note: The text specifically states there was food left over, not a shortfall.

options.text: Elisha refused to distribute the bread at all.
options.note: Elisha explicitly commanded the bread be given to the people to eat.

options.text: The man from Baal-shalishah took the bread back before it could be shared.
options.note: The bread was given to Elisha specifically to be distributed to the people, and it was.

questions: The widow had almost nothing left, just one jar of oil, yet it became enough when placed in God's hands. What small resource do you have that you need to offer to God in faith rather than dismiss as insufficient?

The Shunammite woman refused to say anything was wrong until she reached the man of God, insisting everything is all right even in her grief. Where do you tend to hide your true distress instead of bringing it directly and urgently to God?

Elisha personally and physically identified with the dead child, stretching himself over him, before life returned. How does knowing that Christ fully entered our death shape your hope in your own suffering or grief?

The prophets almost ate poison without realizing it until someone cried out, and only Elisha's intervention made it safe. Where might you need discernment to recognize a hidden danger in your life, and where do you need God's provision to make something right again?

A small gift of twenty loaves fed a hundred men with some left over. What has God given you that seems too small to matter, and how might He be asking you to offer it anyway, trusting Him to multiply it?

translationNotes.note: Debt slavery for a father's unpaid debts was a real ancient Near Eastern and Israelite practice, though the Law of Moses provided limits and eventual release, Exodus 21:2, making Elisha's rescue an act of covenant mercy.

The husband's reference to the New Moon or Sabbath implies these were customary days for visiting a prophet, suggesting the Shunammite's urgent, unscheduled trip signaled something was seriously wrong even before she explained.
The instruction to tie up the garment renders a Hebrew idiom for preparing to move quickly, literally to gird up the loins, matching the urgency of the mission Elisha gives Gehazi.
